Because it is not separate from the mind, it is also called a "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). This is because the object is also the mind; thus, it is analyzed according to these two parts. Alternatively, the intention here is to clarify this by means of three parts:

the cognizing subject is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and the fruit of the valid cognition is the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Their substance is not separate from their function; thus, wisdom itself is named the fruit, because it is that which can cognize the aspect of that seeing-part.
"Aspect" (*nimitta*) refers to the mode of activity (*ākāra*) and the essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); it does not refer to a [physical] mark.
Regarding the differentiation of names and characteristics: those who maintain that there is a manifesting agent possessing functional activity distinguish themselves from the Saṃmitīyas.

According to the latter, the mind grasps its object by directly illuminating and seizing it, like the sun radiating light or like tongs grasping an object. Now, in the Mahāyāna, based on the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), this seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*) arises;

it possesses the capacity to grasp objects, and together with the image division (*nimitta-bhāga*), it serves as the objective condition for the arising of consciousness. This is "conditionality" (*pratyaya*).
This is known to be provisional. Because it has a functional activity that can self-attest its own arising, it is said to "manifest.
This differs from the opponent's adherence to the direct and real apprehension of objects. This self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is also called a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

likewise, either that seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) or this image portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) is also called a valid cognition, because they are not separate from the means of cognition. This is as in the expression "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), which is stated in accordance with conventional discourse.

This explains the three aspects of the meaning. Thus, the *Nyāyamukha* states: "Furthermore, within this [process], there is no separate result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), because this very entity arises as if it were the object, and because it appears to have utility; it is therefore metaphorically designated as 'valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*)."
"Discriminative cognition that functions differently with respect to its object is called 'pseudo-perception' (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Commentary:

This begins the fourth major section, which clarifies the two types of pseudo-valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). It is explained next because it involves defining the true and the pseudo by way of their mutual contrast.

Within this, there are two parts: first, that which resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*); second, that which resembles inference (*anumānābhāsa*). Within the resemblance to direct perception, it is further divided into two:
first, the heading; second, the explanation. This is the first [the heading]. Within the heading, there are three sections: first, the definition of the essence of what resembles direct perception;

second, the definition of the basis for its resemblance; third, the definition of the specific name "resemblance. "Discriminative cognition" refers to [cognition] that carries names, seeds, and so forth, as previously described.
Various conceptual cognitions do not accord with the actual object; because a distinct false understanding arises, they are said to "function differently regarding the referent.
This is called "resembling direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*); this indicates the designation of "semblance."
This means that all cognitions of jars, garments, and so forth arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
[Commentary: The following is the explanation. This explanatory text also consists of three parts; this is the first.

It means that all cognitions which take jars, garments, and so forth as their objects do not correspond to the actual reality of the object, but arise from false conceptual construction. According to the principle, there are five types of cognition.

All these are termed "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). First, the distracted mind taking the past as its object; second, the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking the present as its object;
third, the distracted mind taking the future as its object; fourth, the doubtful cognition taking the three periods of time as its object;

and fifth, the confused cognition taking the present as its object—namely, seeing a tree stump as a person, viewing a mirage as water, or [misconceiving] jars, clothing, and so forth. These are called "confused cognitions" (*bhrāntijñāna*), and none of them constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is subsumed under "semblance" (*pratibhāsa*). Alternatively, it refers to the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and other sentient beings who claim that [their cognition] is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyamukha* states: "In this [cognition], because one apprehends a portion of another object, it is not called direct perception.
Based on this, it is taught that recollection, inference, desire, doubt, deluded cognition, and so forth—such as the cognition of a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*)—are all not direct perception.
Because it evolves according to prior conceptualizations of what is liked, the five cognitions are respectively correlated with the cognition of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth.
The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to that which is directed inward; there is nothing else external to be equated with this. Regarding "the thirst of the deer" (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*) and so forth:
in the Western Regions (Sindh), people commonly call a mirage "the thirst of the deer. Because of their parching heat and thirst, deer perceive it as water and give rise to desire for it.

Therefore, this term "and so forth" [in the phrase "this object and so forth"] refers to cases such as seeing a tree stump and taking it to be a person, or the visual distortions of a diseased eye, such as floating hairs, nets of hair, two moons, vases, garments, and the like. Thus, he further states:

"In this way, regarding all that exists conventionally, cognitions of number, dimension, configuration, existence, and vase-ness with respect to vases and so forth are all similar to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); they are conventional and not ultimate."

This is called conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*). By mentioning "the jar" and so forth, one includes the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the categories of reality (*tattva*), and the category of qualities (*guṇa*) as postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas;

the word "and so forth" includes their [categories of] dimension, conjunction, disjunction, and so on. By mentioning "action," one includes the actions of taking up, setting aside, bending, extending, and moving;

by mentioning "that which is grasped," one includes either those very objects or their movement, with the word "and so forth" applying to the remaining [categories]. As for the nature of existence (*sattā*):...
[The examples include] "the great," "the nature of a jar," and so forth. The "nature of a jar" refers to identity and difference; the "and so forth" includes the term "conjunction" and others.

"Cognition" refers to the cognition that takes these as its objects; all such [cognitions] resemble direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). These all function by constructing other mental aspects (*ākāra*) within the actual objective spheres of the five sense-objects, because they evolve through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by falsely combining with other meanings. Question: Since this cognition that takes jars and the like as its objects is called "resembling" [direct perception],...

Question: Among the three types of cognition—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)—in which are these included? Answer: They are subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Question:

Just as the seventh consciousness, by taking the eighth consciousness as its object, grasps it as a self and may thus be called non-valid cognition, how can that which takes clothes or vases as its objects in a general way be called non-valid cognition when it is not a mind of grasping (*abhiniveśa*)?

Answer: It should be understood that non-valid cognition does not necessarily require a mind of grasping; rather, it is simply any cognition that does not accord with its object and instead forms a different interpretation. Thus, [it is non-valid].

It is called "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*). Although the mind that takes a jar or the like as its object does not necessarily involve conceptual grasping, because it is delusive and conceives [the object] as a real jar, it is therefore non-valid cognition.

Question: Since jars and garments exist, and the cognition that takes them as objects arises, it should be termed "conformative knowledge" (*yathārtha-jñāna*); why then is it called "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*)?
"Because they do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object regarding the referent.

The commentary states: This explains the reason. It is because those various cognitions, with respect to the four types of sensory objects, do not take the specific characteristic as the observed object;

rather, they take as their cognitive object (*ālambana*) something else that is substantially real, which is superimposed upon the aforementioned [objects]. This is called "transforming differently" (*anyathā-vṛtti*).

This [consciousness] takes the entities of jars, clothes, and so forth to be the four sense-objects themselves; it designates "jar" or "clothes" as mere conventional names based upon those four sense-objects.

These possess only common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This cognition does not take the original specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the four sense-objects as its object;
rather, it operates upon these conventional dharmas—jars and clothes—which are merely common characteristics, and regards them as truly existent. Therefore, it is called "partial" (*bhāga*).
"Distinct. This is termed "pseudo-direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

The commentary states: This explains that the name "pseudo" is certain; because those jars and garments are conventionally designated based on the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*), they are apprehended solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

They function through common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). In reality, they are not obtained through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of visual consciousness. To claim that one "sees with the eyes" these things such as jars or garments is called "pseudo-direct perception.

Furthermore, when one merely conceptualizes them as being substantially existent (*dravyasat*) and claims to obtain them through the manifestation of one's own consciousness, this too is called "pseudo-direct perception.
It is not only that which is obtained through what resembles visual direct perception that is termed pseudo-direct perception; this explanation exhausts the meaning.
Because the previous [explanation] was based on the analysis of the term.
If a cognition that appears as an object is produced preceded by a cognition that appears as a similar [object], it is called "pseudo-inference" (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
The commentary states: This second explanation of pseudo-inference also consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. This is the first.

In this regard, there are three parts: first, the indication of the cause; second, the indication of the pseudo-entity (*tattva*); and third, the indication of the pseudo-name. Regarding "pseudo-causal cognition" (*hetu-jñāna*):
it refers to the cognition that takes the pseudo-cause and its conditions as its primary object, which subsequently gives rise to the cognition that realizes the pseudo-proposition (*pakṣa*).

This is termed "pseudo-inference" (*anumāna*). Question: Why is the pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣa*) indicated by its pseudo-entity first, while the pseudo-inference is indicated by its pseudo-cause first? Answer: This is because...
In this context, the cause precedes the effect. To answer that [objection regarding] its resemblance to perception:

because one encounters an object and immediately grasps it as being truly existent, rather than through subsequent inference, the effect is indicated first. This resembles inference (*anumāna*), for which the cause must necessarily exist prior [to the effect].

Subsequently, one engages in speculative investigation; since false wisdom arises thereafter, the cause is presented first. Alternatively, it serves as an implicit illustration: the three phrases and the three meanings are to be explained by assigning them respectively.
"Pseudo-reasons are of many kinds, as previously stated; taking those as reasons [is what is meant].

Commentary: This explains what follows. As previously stated, the nine fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the fourteen fallacies of the reason (*hetu*), and their pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are all causes for the arising of cognition, and are thus collectively termed "pseudo-reasons.
These have already been explained at length; fearing prolixity, I shall merely refer to them here according to the headings.
There is both the object of cognition and the cause. Now, in this explanation, there is also the cause of that which is cognized and the cognition that cognizes it;
since both are incorrect, they are both termed "pseudo-causes" (*hetvābhāsa*). However, although these do not appear in the text of the explanation, they are indicated by citing the cause itself.

Taking that cause and cognition as the primary cause, according to the underlying principle, the heading should also state: "If the pseudo-cause, the cognition thereof, and the erroneous recollection of what has been established..."

The reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*) are inseparable; this is because the preceding text was abbreviated, and thus it remains so here. The commentary follows the headings and likewise omits further explanation.
Regarding the various cognitions that arise with respect to fallacious objects of inference (*sādhyābhāsa*):

The commentary states: This explains the aforementioned cognitions that appear to be objects but are not. "Arising" (*utpāda*) and "being produced" (*jāti*) are identical in meaning though different in wording.

For example, when one falsely perceives mist and the like as smoke, one says that there is a cognition arising with respect to what appears to be an inferable object, namely, the false proof of the presence of fire;
this is expressed as "a cognition is produced."
"Inability to correctly understand is called 'pseudo-inference' (*tarka-anumāna-bhāsa*).
The commentary states: This explains the definition. Because of those fallacious reasons (*hetu*), false cognition arises; one is unable to correctly understand whether that fire exists or not.
Although it belongs to the same category as true inference, because it is not truly so, it is called pseudo-inference.
Furthermore, if one correctly points out the faults of the proof (*sādhana*), it is called refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

[The commentary] states: The fifth major section below explains true refutation. This textual section is divided into three parts: first, a general definition of refutation; second, an analysis of the object of refutation;
and third, a simultaneous demonstration of how it leads others to realization, concluding with the designation of "refutation. Alternatively, it may be divided into four parts.

The first and second [sections] are as before. The third reveals the essence of the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). The fourth concludes the name of the refutation. Alternatively, the former is the heading and the latter is the explanation.

Within the heading, there are three parts: first, correctly demonstrating the essence of the refutation; second, indicating the faults of the proof (*sādhana*); and third, indicating the object of the refutation, which is designated as "the refutation.
Following this, the name of the refutation is indicated. In the subsequent explanation, the object comes first, followed by the essence, and finally—

Regarding the name: for now, we shall follow the first section, which is this very one. To know another's position as it truly is, with the aim of making them realize its error, is what constitutes "naming.
If one correctly demonstrates the faults of the proof (*sādhana*), what are those faults?

This refers to the nature of defects in the initial proof, namely: the defect of deficiency in the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*), the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*), the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), and the defect of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*).

The commentary states: This identifies the objects of refutation; thus, the faults in the opponent's formulation are divided into two parts. First, the deficiency of members (*aṅga-nyūna*) is analyzed; next, [the other faults] are explained.

The first fault refers to the deficiency in the initial *sādhana* (proof). This refers to the first analysis of the omission of members (*aṅga-nyūna*): either the total absence of words, or words that lack meaning.

Because this fault is more serious, it is explained first; hence it is called "the first. Regarding this deficiency, ancient masters categorized it according to the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*), resulting in seven or six cases.
From Dignāga onwards, it was categorized according to the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) of the reason, also resulting in six cases.

Seven. These are all distinguished as before. Alternatively, if we provisionally take Dignāga’s three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) to constitute seven propositions, there are three cases where one [characteristic] is missing.
For example, as when a Sāṃkhya teacher argues against a Vaiyākaraṇa that sound is impermanent because it is visible to the eye.
In the thesis that "sound is impermanent," jars, colors, bowls, and so forth serve as similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while space and so forth serve as dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

This [reason] lacks the first characteristic but possesses the latter two. When the proponents of sound (*śabdavādin*) oppose the Sarvāstivādins by establishing the thesis that "sound is permanent" because it has the nature of being audible, space serves as the common similar instance, while jars, bowls, and so forth serve as the dissimilar instances; this [reason] lacks the second characteristic, namely, being an object of cognition (*prameya*).
The essential cause (*svabhāvahetu*) lacks the third characteristic. Regarding the case where two [characteristics] are lacking while one remains:

for example, when establishing that "sound is not produced by effort (*aprayatnaja*)," because it is perceived by the nose, space (*ākāśa*) and the like serve as similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while jars, basins, and the like serve as dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). This lacks the first two characteristics.

For example, when establishing "the self (*ātman*) is eternal" against a Buddhist opponent, the reason given is "it is not produced by volitional effort. Here, space serves as the similar instance, while lightning and the like serve as the dissimilar instances. This is the reason.

Because the basis [of the reason] is lacking, the first characteristic is absent. In cases such as "lightning and so forth," the third characteristic is absent. Regarding the four contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*), the latter two characteristics are likewise lacking.

For example, if one were to establish that "sound is eternal because it is visible to the eye," with space as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), all three characteristics would be entirely absent.
Following the section on "the faults of the thesis and so forth" (*pakṣadoṣādi*), the faults of the individual members [of the syllogism] are explained separately. These, or...
The name of the "refuted" (*dūṣya*) is established for the "refuter" (*dūṣaṇa*). Thus, the *Nyāyamukha* states:

"In this context, those [statements] such as 'deficient' (*nyūna*) and so forth that constitute the refutation refer to the aforementioned deficiencies in the words and members [of the proof]. Each of these individual statements is called a 'refutation.
Alternatively, the name 'refuter' is established for the 'refuted. Furthermore, the *Nyāyamukha* asks: "What is the characteristic of the similar instance (*sādharmya*)?"
It resembles a refutation because it speaks of a "refuter" in relation to the act of refuting, and because it is traditionally understood as such. Thus it is said. Question:
Why are deficiencies in the proof (*sādhana*) and so forth called "refutations" (*dūṣaṇa*)? Answer: Because the logic of a refutation lies in the utterance that points out those faults.
To this we reply: here, the term for the "refuted" (*dūṣya*) is applied to the "refuter" (*dūṣaṇa*); in reality, however, the refutation resides in the speech itself.

Alternatively, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) may be applied to that which is produced. Deficiencies in the proof (*sādhana*), such as the lack of a reason (*hetu*), are called the "agents" because they give rise to these words of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Thus, the words of refutation arise from those [deficiencies] which appear as such; this is what is meant by "the produced" (*kārya*).

"Arising," "being born," and "producing" differ in name but are identical in meaning. The actual refutation resides in the words; when one says that the proof is deficient, etc., this constitutes the refutation.

The name "producer" (*kāraṇa*) is established based on that which is produced (*kārya*), just as the designation of a cause is established with respect to its effect. Alternatively, this may refer solely to the object;
for it will be stated below that these words "reveal" (*saṃdarśana*). If the former [explanation] were already sufficient, why would the latter need to be stated?
It is called "capable of refuting" (*dūṣaṇa*) because it displays these words in order to enlighten the questioner.

[The commentary] states: This also demonstrates the realization of others, thereby establishing the designation of "refutation. When faults arise in the proponent's position, the opponent censures the proponent's error.

Regarding the phrase "the one who questions both the proof and the establishment of its fault," what is meant by "the questioner"? It is the opponent who is able to correctly point out deficiencies and other such flaws; it is not [the proponent].

The illumination present in speech is called "demonstration" (*pradarśana*). This occurs through the power of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), which brings about the realization for the questioner, causing them to recognize their error, abandon the false, and proceed toward the true.
This is what is meant by "awakening others," and it is termed "refutation. Thus, this simultaneously clarifies the awakening of others.

This explains the meaning of the term "capable refuter" (*sādhana-bhūta-dūsaka*). Although one may refute another, if it does not cause that other to realize the truth, it is not considered a "capable refuter.

Furthermore, there are cases where establishing a formal inference (*prayoga*) to refute another is called a "capable refuter. Here, for the time being, we define a "capable refuter" as one who refutes another by exposing their faults;
or rather, because the opponent's own established inference contains a fault, one subsequently establishes an inference to refute them, which thereby also reveals those faults. Therefore...
[This] encompasses all [fallacies]. If the opponent is without fault, a refutation that is merely similar [to a valid one] is not a genuine refutation.
If one expresses words that point out a fault in the proof (*sādhana*) when no such fault actually exists, it is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
The commentary states: This sixth major section clarifies fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*). The text is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of fallacious refutations;

second, the exposition of the nature of fallacious refutation; and third, the conclusion regarding the name of fallacious refutation, along with an explanation of its rationale. This is the first part.
This refers to the statement regarding a complete proof (*sādhana*) that reaches the point of having a faulty example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*).

The commentary states: this sets forth the nature of the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) by means of an example. First, it clarifies the deficiency of false speech; subsequently, it distinguishes correct speech, which is the completeness of the opponent’s measure (*pramāṇa*).

False speech possesses deficiencies, whereas the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are correct. To falsely claim something is wrong when it is not, or to fail to understand its truth, is what is meant here.

To speak with self-assurance based on what is established in opposition to the true [refutation] is called a "pseudo-refutation. This can be fully understood by reflecting upon it in comparison to a true refutation.
Such discourse is termed a pseudo-refutation.

The commentary states: The following concludes the designation of "pseudo-refutation" and explains the reason for it. This section is divided into two parts: the conclusion and the explanation; this is the first.
The term "thus" (*evam*) refers back to what precedes. "Discourse" (*vacana*) refers to complete proofs, deficient statements, and so forth.
Such expressions as these are called "pseudo-refutations. Question: Why [is this said] regarding the complete [proof]?
The *sādhana* (proof) [is like a pseudo-refutation] because it displays defects such as incompleteness in the statement, etc., and thus acts as a pseudo-refutation;
for it cannot reveal the faults of the opponent’s position, since that [opponent] is without fault.
The commentary states: this explains the reason. Now, one who refutes [properly] points out the faults in what the other has established exactly as they are, thereby revealing them.

Establishing proof serves to make known the opponent's faults and is capable of generating that [correct] knowledge; thus, it possesses the power to awaken others and may be termed "capable refutation.

Since the opponent is actually without fault, yet falsely raises objections, they are unable to manifest the defects of the other's position. Why? Because they are unable to manifest that [position] as being without fault.
Furthermore, they do not know the opponent's faults as they truly are, and they falsely [impute faults] to those points that are not defective.
Śaṅkara objects: This, too, cannot manifest another’s fault, because there is no fault [to be found].

To establish a fallacy of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not truly capable of demonstrating [the opponent's error], yet it appears as if it could refute them. Now, based on what is certain, we shall set forth the true means of establishment (*samyak-sādhana*).
Let us cease this matter for now.
The commentary states: In the third major section, the cardinal directions are briefly indicated to avoid excessive prolixity. These eight meanings discussed in the treatise are truly numerous;
they are summarized briefly as eight, though expanded upon through their full manifestation. Fearing that there may be no gradual progress toward them, I shall now [proceed].
To speak briefly: let this matter rest for now.

Having already proclaimed a few words of meaning as a beginning to establish the general direction, the subtle distinctions between what is logical and what is illogical therein shall be discerned in other places.
The commentary states: Within this treatise, the text is divided into two parts; this is the second, which reveals the brief summary and points toward the extensive explanation. Above...

The first two lines present the summary; the following two lines point to the detailed exposition. The brief proclamation, as previously stated, consists of a few words and meanings intended to establish the basic framework for beginners.

Regarding the eight topics, the principles of what is rational and what is irrational have been extensively and exquisitely analyzed in works such as the *Nyāyamukha*, the *Hetumukha*, and the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
Although I, Zhao, have been placed upon the ranks of the Dharma, my decayed sentiments are difficult to refine. Having unworthily assumed this office by succession, I am unable to diminish my words.

Regarding the Master, I once obtained half of his extraordinary transmission; yet due to circumstances, I have not yet received the full treasure. On the occasion of these instructions, I shall raise a firefly to assist the light of the sun.
As for the correctness or error of the principles and phrasing therein, I pray that those possessed of wisdom will graciously examine and determine them.

In the second year of the Hōgen era, at the regular lecture assembly of Zenshō-ji Temple, while discussing the Great Commentary on the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, we reached the passage in the commentary beginning with "the unestablishedness of the probans" (*sādhanābhāva*).
The various manuscript versions differed; some added text upon existing text, leading to errors through arbitrary selection and omission, or...
The character "zhǐ" (止) beneath the characters [of the title] contains many errors. Nevertheless, for now, we shall provisionally rely on the Tang dynasty *Huìlùn* masters.
Furthermore, according to the humble examination of this neophyte, there are two versions of the *Jiàngshù* (Commentary): first, that composed by Cí'ēn (Cien), such as the *Míngquán Dǎoshù*;
second, the continuation from Zīzhōu (Zizhou), which is the commentary currently being transcribed. The original text of the former is brief and its principles narrow; the latter...

The commentary’s phrasing is extensive and its meaning is rich. To add further text would be to have what was originally absent; though one might obtain half a jewel, the whole treasure remains unseen.

Yet, even with only a single passage, the original is complete while the later additions are lacking. For instance, regarding the statement "as subsumed by valid cognition," this serves to exclude the fault of being indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).

The wording differs between teacher and disciple; do not arbitrarily alter or delete it. The commentary distinguishes between the fundamental and the derivative, without leaning toward either the right or the wrong.
Thus it was.
At that time, on the seventh day of the third month of the spring in the third year of the same era, the Great Dharma Master Zangjun recorded this.

Now, having compared the various records of Tang and He, [it is seen that] regarding the section from "The capacity to establish is not established" onwards, there is the commentary by Youji and the continuation by Zhizhao. This clarifies [the matter].
The *Xuan Dao-shu* was composed by Ji; the commentary currently transcribed here is a continuation by Zhao. The *Yao-yi-chao* states:

"In the initial syllogism of Ji’s commentary, it does not say 'the object of inference is universally established' (*prasiddha-anumāna*), but simply says 'it is not the object of perception or inference,' implying that one part is not universally established.

The *Zhi-xu* states: "[It refers to] the object of inference that is universally established. Regarding the subject (*dharmin*) of the subsequent syllogism, both Ji’s commentary and Zhao’s continuation agree.
[The text] says: "That which is universally established as manifest is a portion that is not universally established as a means of valid cognition" (end of citation).
Myōsen states: "Regarding the statement 'taking that [which is] obstructive and attributing it to impermanence,' Master Chō says:
'Taking that impermanence and attributing it to the obstructive' (and so forth). The rest of the text is the same" (end of citation). Myōtōshō states: "The text can resolve that difficulty."
Regarding the "Master’s Explanation of the Difficulties Concerning Separation and Union": this is the additional text from Master Tz’ao’s new supplementary commentary (end quote).

Zhou’s Record and [Zhuo] Ba’s Record clearly explain that the meaning of the upper and lower sections is identical. However, some people, seeing the note in the commentary stating, "The latter portion is missing; I have not yet obtained it;

However, the *Damingdeng chao* states: "As for the *Wenlun*, which establishes the doctrine, it was continued by Huizhao.
The commentary notes: 'Later [the text] was missing; he had not yet obtained [it], having only acquired half a pearl. There are some versions of the sub-commentary that lack this passage.

Based on the words of Master Huizhao at the end of this fascicle, that text says: 'From my teacher, I once obtained half a pearl; due to circumstances being lacking, I have not yet received the complete jewel.'"
From this one may infer that Master Zao’s own commentary consists of three fascicles; having already devoted myself to it, I have now examined these three fascicles.
As for the remaining two and a half fascicles, since more than half is already complete, how can it be called "half"? A whole cannot be termed "half" merely because it is not complete;

why must it be divided into equal parts to be called "half"? As the preface to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "However, of this entire canon, I have obtained barely thirty thousand words; it has only just begun to be opened..."

A half-jewel. One has not yet beheld the complete treasure. It is said that this sutra’s lower version contains one hundred thousand verses, whereas the version obtained during the Jin dynasty consists of only thirty-six thousand verses.
What was acquired is still meager; it barely amounts to half, yet even so, it is considered but a half-jewel.
The present case is likewise so; it is not called "complete," but merely "half" (and so forth). The subsequent text states:

"Regarding the master from whom he once obtained half a pearl, due to a deficiency in conditions, he did not receive the full jewel. There is a commentary on the Tang edition which says: "The proponent’s argument is unestablished;

the final note states that later, due to a deficiency, he failed to obtain [the whole] and only acquired half a pearl" (end quote). The Preface to the Revised Edition states: "Since he was pressed by the matter of the half-pearl..."

My feelings have thus led me to harbor the hope of capturing the *qilin*. Now, my intention being such, as for the statement that "conditions are lacking," does this mean it was for the sake of a teacher or a patron?
I do not know what the reason is (and so forth). This text seems to lack a foundational commentary (*shu*), yet there is no subsequent addition;
therefore, I have made these remarks in the same manner as a commentary (*zhù*) on the *shu*.
